questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Equation Given a Complex Root and Its Leading Coefficient
questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-1+\sqrt{3}\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $4$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=-1+\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(-1+\sqrt{3}\text{i}))(x-(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i})-x(-1+\sqrt{3}\text{i})+(-1-\sqrt{3}\text{i})(-1+\sqrt{3}\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+x+\sqrt{3}x\text{i}+x-\sqrt{3}x\text{i}+1-3{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+1+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=-1\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $4.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $4.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}^{2}+2x+4) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+8x+16 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-\frac{2\text{i}}{3}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $-27,$ find the equation. Write your answer in the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0,$ where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are real constants.

{{field-1}}$=0$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=-\frac{2\text{i}}{3}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=\frac{2\text{i}}{3}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-\frac{2\text{i}}{3})(x+\frac{2\text{i}}{3})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{(\frac{2\text{i}}{3})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{4}{9}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{4}{9} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \frac{2\text{i}}{3},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $-27.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $-27.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-27({x}^{2}+\frac{4}{9}) & =0 \\ -27{x}^{2}-12 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

(x-\frac{\sqrt{6}\,\text{i}}{4})(x+\frac{\sqrt{6}\,\text{i}}{4})=0
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{(\frac{\sqrt{6}\,\text{i}}{4})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{6}{16}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{3}{8} & =0.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Equation Given a Complex Root and Its Leading Coefficient
questions.problem:
A quadratic equation with real coefficients has a complex root $x=-2+\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $1,$ find the equation. Write your answer in the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0,$ where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are real constants.

{{field-1}}$=0$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=-2+\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}$ is a root, we know that its complex conjugate $x=-2-\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}$ is also a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(-2+\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}))(x-(-2-\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(-2+\sqrt{7}\,\text{i})-x(-2-\sqrt{7}\,\text{i})+(-2+\sqrt{7}\,\text{i})(-2-\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x-\cancel{x\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}}+2x+\cancel{x\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}}+4-7{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+4x+4+7 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+4x+11 & =0\end{aligned}
$$
